title: What is known about 1RB1RF_1LC0RE_1RD0LC_0LB0RA_1LD1RD_1RB---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RF_1LC0RE_1RD0LC_0LB0RA_1LD1RD_1RB---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and reduced to a counter with no assumption left. Write x = 1110 and a = 10. Most of the time the tape is C> 0 10 x^n0 [1 a^d1 x^n1] ... [1 a^dk x^nk] 1: blocks of x with a ternary digit d in front of each. One round trip of the head is a ternary decrement: the first nonzero digit drops by one, the zeros below it become 2, every block the borrow passes loses one x and the first block gains one. When the counter runs out a new round starts with one more block. Every rule is proved in Lean for all sizes, and the machine halts from blank tape if and only if the counter model reaches a halting pattern: the borrow meeting an empty block followed by a block with digit 0 (halts_iff_model, kernel-checked). Since 12 November the theorem has no hypothesis: the model is a function defined on every list of blocks, including the patterns that never show up in the run, and each of its cases is proved to be what the machine does. The model has run 332,875 rounds (more than 10292 steps) without halting. A halt needs a charged pair of blocks, two neighbours whose block length and digit do not match mod 3 (Lean, good_not_halt). A round-skipping simulator, tested round by round against the exact model for 60,000 rounds, has followed the model to round 33,199,619 without a halt. The run has carried one such pair since round 49,668 (observed), and the model halts if that pair's block runs out before the block after it; sizes say this is not about to happen, but nothing is proved about the long run.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 72,272 cells have been visited and 53,480 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: power/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.545). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.155).

claims.title: Sweep rules
claims.text:
The head sweeps over long runs of a repeated word, rewriting each copy, for any number n of copies and any surrounding tape. Examples:
  • L D> (1011)^n R → L (0101)^n D> R
  • L E> (1101)^n R → L (1010)^n E> R
  • L B> (1110)^n R → L (0101)^n B> R
  • L A> (0111)^n R → L (1010)^n A> R
Generated by py/rules.py (tools/py/bbtools/symtm.py).

claims.title: One bounce is a ternary decrement
claims.text: From C> 0 10 x^n0 [1 x^(m1+1)] ... [1 x^(mj+1)] [1 a^(e+1) x^n] rest (blank to the left, any tape after) the machine reaches C> 0 10 x^(n0+1) [1 a^2 x^m1] ... [1 a^2 x^mj] [1 a^e x^n] rest, for every n0, every list of passed blocks m1..mj, every n, every digit e + 1 ≥ 1 and every rest. In words: the first nonzero digit drops by one, the blocks before it lose one x each and get digit 2, the front block gains one x. Proved by induction over the passed blocks from pieces written by py/counter.py; nothing is assumed.

claims.title: The other rules of the counter
claims.text: Empty blocks (0,0) at the right end: one is removed, two stay (an endless supply of borrows), three become (1,0). A round ends when every digit is 0: (n0; (0,m1+1), ..., (0,mk+1)) becomes (0; (1,n0+1), (0,m1+1), ..., (0,mk), (0,0)), and with no block at all (n0; ) becomes (0; (1,n0), (0,0)). An empty block followed by a block with digit 1 is one more x (a merge, an equality of tapes). The borrow meeting an empty block followed by a nonempty block with digit 0 (or by an empty block and then such a block, or by two empty blocks and anything more) halts the machine. New on 12 November, the cases that never occur in the run: the borrow meeting one or two empty blocks followed by a block with digit e + 2 makes the machine turn round as at the end of a round, (n0; Z, (0,0), (e+2,n), rest) → (0; (1,n0+1), Z, (0,0), (e,n), rest) with the passed blocks Z unchanged. All proved for every size; nothing is assumed.

claims.title: Halting from blank tape is exactly halting of the counter model (no assumption)
claims.text: bounceM is the counter model as a function on every state (n0; list of blocks): it returns the next state or halt. Proved: it never fails to give an answer (bounceM_ne_stuck: the third value stuck of its result type is never returned); a next is a run of the machine of at least one step (bounceM_next); a halt is a halting configuration (bounceM_halt); and blank tape reaches the counter (0; (1,5), (0,0)) at step 403 (blank_to_counter). Hence, in plain words: the machine halts from blank tape if and only if repeating the model's bounce from (0; (1,5), (0,0)) reaches halt (halts_iff_model : HaltsFromBlank ↔ ∃ k, runM k (next 0 [(1,5),(0,0)]) = halt). Nothing is assumed: the earlier version needed the hypothesis that the model never meets an undefined pattern; that hypothesis is gone because every pattern is now defined and proved.

claims.title: The model is the machine's run, bounce by bounce
claims.text: At all 87,809 visits of the head in C to the left end up to step 4·109, the tape read by c/cdump.c is the counter the model predicts (py/model.py check).

claims.title: The model agrees with the machine on random states
claims.text: On 3,000 random lists of blocks (digits 0 to 3, including every pattern that does not occur in the run) one bounce of the Python transcription of the model gives the tape the machine itself reaches, or a halt exactly when the machine halts (py/model.py random 3000). This is a check of the transcription; the Lean theorem does not depend on it.

claims.title: No halt for 332,875 rounds of the model
claims.text: The model with many bounces applied at once (py/model.py far; the jumps checked against single bounces for 300,000 bounces) runs 332,875 rounds in 880 s, about 10292 bounces (each at least one machine step), without halting or getting stuck. The list grows to 608 blocks. The last block ran out with odd size, starting the endless-supply phase, only twice (rounds 23 and 49,668).

claims.title: A halt needs a charged pair of blocks
claims.text: Call two neighbouring blocks (d, n), (d', n') neutral when n ≡ d' + 2 (mod 3) and charged otherwise. In a neutral pair an empty block is followed by a digit 1 and the two merge, while every halting pattern starts with an empty block followed by a digit 0. Proved: if every pair of the list is neutral, the next bounce of the model is not a halt, for every n0. The pairs behind the empty blocks that the end of a round leaves at the very end of the list are exempt, so the end of the list needs no argument about sizes.

claims.title: Where a charge can be made (all small states)
claims.text: On every list of up to 6 blocks with digits below 3 and block lengths below 5 in which every pair is neutral (230,592 states): the next bounce is not a halt; if n0 + d<sub>1</sub> ≡ 1 (mod 3), every pair is neutral afterwards too; and n0 + d<sub>1</sub> ≡ 1 is kept unless the first block ran out and merged into the front block in that bounce. A charged pair is made only at the end of a round, when n0 ≡ 1 (mod 3) fails. Checked by enumeration, not proved for all sizes.

claims.title: The run carries a charged pair since round 49,668
claims.text: In the model's run from blank tape the first block runs out in rounds 22, 183 and 49,668. The first two leave n0 right by the end of the round. In round 49,668 the last block runs out at the end of a round, two empty blocks stay at the end and supply borrows without end, and while the counter wraps round the whole front of the list runs out; round 49,669 starts with one charged pair (residue 1). It is still there at round 255,000, on a block of about 1.3·10<sup>113</sup> copies of x, 214th from the right end.

claims.title: What the charge means for halting
claims.text: If the charged block runs out while the block after it is not empty, the borrow finds an empty block followed by a digit 0: the model halts. A block with p − 1 blocks to its right loses 3<sup>p−1</sup> per round, so the charged block would last 3·10<sup>11</sup> rounds and its right neighbour 1.9·10<sup>11</sup>: the neighbour would go first, and the charged block is also fed by the young blocks that run out on its left. Nothing is proved about the long run. A round-skipping run to round 33,199,619 (next claim) saw one event behind the charged block, after which both blocks last 9 times longer: 2.7·10<sup>12</sup> and 1.7·10<sup>12</sup> rounds, the neighbour still first. The earlier guess on this page, that a halt would come from the end of the list, is withdrawn.

claims.title: No halt of the counter model in 33,199,619 rounds (round-skipping run)
claims.text: py/skip.py stores the blocks at the right end as a size and a rate (the block with q blocks to its right loses exactly 3q per round, the last one 2) and runs only the young blocks at the front bounce by bounce; rounds with an event are done by the exact model, which alone can report a halt. Tested against the exact model at every round start up to round 60,000 (through the collapse of round 49,668) and for 3,000 rounds from round 100,000. Observed: no halt up to round 33,199,619; in round 19,080,842 the second block from the right end ran out and the last three blocks merged into one, making no new charge; the one charged pair is now 212th from the right end.

claims.title: Conserved differences
claims.text: Counting blocks from the right end, per round block p loses 3<sup>p-1</sup> (the last loses 2), so the differences n<sub>p+1</sub> − 3n<sub>p</sub> (p ≥ 2) do not change between merges. That is why the blocks at the right end run out together, in rare collapses (rounds 23 and 49,668 so far).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. Equivalent (in Lean, with no assumption) to the counter model reaching its halting pattern. A halt needs a charged pair of blocks (Lean); the run has carried one since round 49,668 and still has exactly one at round 33,199,619 (observed), and the model halts if its block runs out before the block after it. Whether that ever happens is a question about sizes, like a Collatz problem.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows, but the question is now a question about a counter. Each round trip of the head is a ternary decrement, proved in Lean for every size, the machine halts exactly when this counter meets one pattern, and that pattern needs a pair of blocks that is out of step mod 3. This page runs the real machine in your browser and lets you run the counter.

facts.text: Proved in Lean: halting from blank tape is halting of an explicit counter model.
Proved in Lean: a list whose pairs all match mod 3 does not halt at the next bounce.
The model and the C simulator agree at every bounce to 4·10<sup>9</sup> steps.
No halt in 332,875 rounds of the model.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.

sections.heading: The tape is a ternary counter
html:
Write x for 1110 and a for 10. Whenever the head, in C, is at the left end of the tape, the tape reads

C> 0 10 x^n0 [1 a^d1 x^n1] [1 a^d2 x^n2] ... [1 a^dk x^nk] 1

a first block of x, then k groups, each a separator 1, a digit d (zero, one or two copies of a) and a block of x. Write the state as (n0; (d1,n1), ..., (dk,nk)). Consecutive visits, from step 2,297:

step 2,297   (2; (2,10), (2,1), (2,0))
step 2,345   (3; (1,10), (2,1), (2,0))
step 2,407   (4; (0,10), (2,1), (2,0))
step 2,625   (5; (2,9),  (1,1), (2,0))
step 2,715   (6; (1,9),  (1,1), (2,0))
step 2,819   (7; (0,9),  (1,1), (2,0))
step 3,065   (8; (2,8),  (0,1), (2,0))

The digits count down in base 3, least significant first: 222, 122, 022, 212, 112, 012, 202, ... Each time the borrow passes a group, the group loses one x; the first block gains one x per visit.

sections.heading: One round trip is one decrement
html:
From the left end, C sweeps right, turning the x of the first block and of every group with digit 0 into pairs a, until it reaches the first nonzero digit. It removes one a there, and the head zig-zags back to the left end: each zig-zag eats two a on its left and leaves one x on its right, so the blocks are rebuilt, one x shorter, with digit 2 in front:

C> 0 10 x^n0 [1 x^(m1+1)] ... [1 x^(mj+1)] [1 a^(e+1) x^n] rest
  → C> 0 10 x^(n0+1) [1 a^2 x^m1] ... [1 a^2 x^mj] [1 a^e x^n] rest

This is proved in Lean for every n0, n, e and every list of passed groups, with any tape after (bounce_gen): six pieces found by the symbolic simulator and an induction over the groups.

sections.heading: Rounds, and why the blocks shrink by powers of 3
html:
A round starts with every digit equal to 2, so the counter holds 3m − 1 for m groups. Counting down to 0, group i is passed once for every multiple of 3i on the way, 3m−i − 1 times. When every digit is 0 the borrow runs off the end; the head converts the tape back, and the next round starts with one more group in front, of size 3m + 1 (all proved: exhaust). In one formula, with the blocks c1, ..., cm at the start of a round:

(c1, ..., cm)  →  (3^m + 1, c1 − 3^(m−1), c2 − 3^(m−2), ..., c(m−1) − 3, cm − 2)

That is the "geometric decrements" seen in the plain run: at the right end the blocks of pairs 10 (2 per x) lose 4, 6, 18, 54, 162, ... per round, and the front block is 5 + 2·3m = 1463, 4379, 13127, ...

sections.heading: Merges and the end of the list
html:
A block smaller than its decrement runs out during the round. Once empty it becomes (2,0), then (1,0), then (0,0), just 1. An empty group followed by a group with digit 1 reads 1 1 10 = 1110: one more x, so the two groups join the block before them (a merge, an identity of tapes). This keeps the list at 5 to 9 groups for the first 1010 steps; later it grows slowly (608 groups after 332,875 rounds of the model).

Empty groups at the right end act as extra digits: one is used up, two stay forever (an endless supply of borrows, the "A phase", which lasts until the last group runs out), three become (1,0). The last group loses 2 per round; it starts an A phase only if it runs out with odd size, which happened twice in 332,875 rounds.

sections.heading: Where a halt would come from
html:
The machine halts (F reading 1) exactly when the borrow meets an empty group (0,0) followed by a nonempty group with digit 0, or by an empty group and then such a group, or by two empty groups and anything more: proved (bounce_halt). And that is the only way: the machine halts from blank tape if and only if the counter model reaches that pattern (halts_iff_model, checked by Lean's kernel, nothing assumed). The model is a function defined on every list of groups. For the patterns that have never occurred in the run it was proved what the machine does: for example, if the borrow meets an empty group followed by a group with digit 2, the machine turns round right there, as it does at the end of a round, and the digit 2 becomes 0 — which is the halting pattern two bounces later unless that group is empty too.

Which lists can reach that pattern? The next section answers half of it: only lists with a charged pair, and the run has had one since round 49,668. No halt in 332,875 rounds, about 10292 steps.

sections.heading: Charged pairs: what a halt needs
html: Take two neighbouring groups (d, n) and (d', n'): a digit and a block length each. Call the pair neutral when n ≡ d' + 2 (mod 3), and charged otherwise. A decrement lowers n and d' together (or neither), so a pair keeps its residue n − d' − 2 (mod 3) for as long as both groups exist.

In a neutral pair, a block that has run out (n = 0) is followed by a digit 1, and those two groups simply merge. Every halting pattern starts with an empty group followed by a digit 0. So: a halt needs a charged pair. This is proved in Lean for every list (good_not_halt): if all pairs are neutral, the next bounce is not a halt. The empty groups that the end of a round leaves at the very end of the list are exempt (shown as · below), so the end of the list, which the earlier version of this page suspected, is harmless.

Run the counter and watch the pairs. Each chip is a group, digit | block length; between two chips is the residue of the pair: 0 neutral, +1 or +2 charged. One bounce is one round trip of the machine's head (the model proved in Lean, transcribed to JavaScript and tested against the Python model on 20,000 random lists).

Where a charge comes from. The only new pair is the one made at the end of a round, between the new first group (1, n0+1) and the old one, and it is neutral exactly when the front block has n0 ≡ 1 (mod 3). The relation n0 + d1 ≡ 1 holds from the start and survives every bounce except one in which the first group runs out and merges into the front block. (Checked on all 230,592 neutral lists of up to 6 small groups; not proved for all sizes.)

In the real run (observed, not proved): the first group runs out in rounds 22, 183 and 49,668. The first two are repaired before the round ends. In round 49,668 the last group runs out exactly at the end of a round; two empty groups then sit at the end and hand out borrows without end, the counter wraps round millions of times, and the whole front of the list runs out. Round 49,669 starts with one charged pair, of residue 1, and it is still there at round 255,000. Its block holds about 1.3·10113 copies of x and sits 214th from the right end.

What it means. If that block ever runs out while the group after it is not empty, the model, and so the machine, halts. A group with p − 1 groups to its right loses 3p−1 per round; at that rate the charged block would last 3·1011 rounds and its right neighbour 1.9·1011, so the neighbour would go first, and the charged block is also fed by the young groups that run out on its left. That is a forecast from sizes, not a proof, and with more than 3200 bounces per round no simulator we have can follow it. The halting question is now: does a charged block ever run out before its right neighbour?

Followed further (observed). A simulator that skips the untouched blocks at the right end (py/skip.py, tested round by round against the exact model for 60,000 rounds) has taken the model to round 33,199,619 without a halt. In round 19,080,842 the second block from the right end ran out and the last three blocks merged into one. That left the charged pair in place, 212th from the right end instead of 214th, and made both of its blocks lose 9 times less per round: the charged block would now last 2.7·1012 rounds and the block after it 1.7·1012. So the race is still open, and events at the right end keep moving the finishing line. Nothing here is proved.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.545). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.155).
After 109 steps the tape spans 72,272 cells (52,864 left of the start, 125 right), with a density of 1s of 0.74.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

summary: A ternary counter: each round trip of the head decrements a base-3 counter whose digits sit between blocks of x = 1110, and every block the borrow passes loses one x. Proved in Lean (kernel): the machine halts from blank tape iff an explicit counter model halts, and a halt needs a 'charged' pair of blocks (lengths and digits mismatched mod 3). Observed: the run has carried one charged pair since round 49,668; no halt in 33,199,619 rounds of the counter model. Open, Collatz-like.
